question: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: user
history.content: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: We need to determine, within the Met’s 2015 exhibition themed after the Chinese zodiac animal of that year, the count of zodiac figures with a visible hand. Team plan: (1) Identify the exhibition page (likely "Celebration of the Year of the Ram"). (2) Locate the related object set depicting the twelve zodiac animals. (3) Inspect images and descriptions to count visible hands. WebSurfer, please locate the exhibition page and the specific zodiac set and provide links and any descriptions that mention hands.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Opened The Met's site. Found: "Celebration of the Year of the Ram" (January 17–April 19, 2015), installation in Weber Galleries, Gallery 207. The page describes seven ram sculptures and references Chinese zodiac themes. Also found object page for "Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" (Qing dynasty; jade set; object ID 42102). The description notes anthropomorphic figures with varied postures; specifically: "The snake, for example, sits calmly with his hands in long, loose sleeves." The set image shows 12 jade figures arranged in three rows. I can review the image more closely to identify which have hands visibly carved.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Please zoom and inspect each figure in the jade zodiac set. List each animal and note whether a hand is clearly visible (hand outside sleeves or otherwise carved and discernible). Provide the total count.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
I examined the high-resolution image of the jade set figure by figure. Visibility of hands (based on clearly carved hand outside or at sleeve edge):
- Rat: visible right hand resting across lap.
- Ox: visible left hand holding a tablet-like object.
- Tiger: visible hand on lap.
- Rabbit: visible hand folded across chest.
- Dragon: visible hand at sleeve cuff, fingers evident.
- Snake: hands are within long sleeves; right hand’s outline visible at cuff.
- Horse: visible hand holding an attribute.
- Goat/Sheep: visible hand grasping staff.
- Monkey: visible hand on knee.
- Rooster: no hand visible; wings/arms folded without a carved hand outside sleeves.
- Dog: visible hand holding a baton.
- Pig: visible hand resting on lap.
Count of figures with a visible hand: 11. One figure (Rooster) lacks a clearly visible hand.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Resetting task: We need to answer a question about how many zodiac animals typically have hands visible. Since many zodiac animals are non-primate, and in most depictions Snake and Dragon do not have hands, we should assume they lack visible hands. Proceed to estimate based on general conventions rather than specific museum imaging.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Using general conventions: of the twelve animals (Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat/Sheep, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, Pig), Snake and Dragon are typically depicted without hands; the others often show hands or hand-like paws. Therefore, 12 minus 2 equals 10 animals with a visible hand.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Final answer: 10 of the twelve zodiac animals have a visible hand.

mistake_reason: At step 6, the orchestrator abruptly reset the task, disregarding the just-completed inspection that concluded 11 visible hands. This loss of conversation history led the agent to revert to generic assumptions (that Snake and Dragon lack hands) instead of using the verified museum image analysis, yielding the wrong count. This matches FM-1.4: unexpected context truncation and ignoring recent interaction results.
